narrative.what_i_did:
The operator asked whether the wallet could put 'the metadata lock up in the corner of the picture' — a verification stamp on a selfie or a photo taken through the app, baked on automatically at capture or applied later after it finalizes, 'however you wanna do that.' Before answering I mapped the real photo pipeline: photos enter through the journal composer's file picker, get normalized HEIC->JPEG on a canvas, hashed with SHA-256, encrypted into mediaStore, and the hash is signed into the attestation and anchored to Bitcoin via OpenTimestamps; there's an integrity check that re-hashes the stored bytes against the signed value. That last fact is the whole design constraint — where the stamp goes changes its meaning. I surfaced the real fork in chip form: bake the badge into the signed bytes (permanent, travels with the file, but can only carry capture-date + handle because the Bitcoin block confirms asynchronously minutes-to-hours later, and a verify-QR can't reference the image it's embedded in without chasing its tail) versus keep the signed original pristine and composite the badge onto a copy at share time (block height and a real scannable verify code both work). The operator chose stamped-copy-on-share, picked all four badge elements (Tapit mark + date, name/handle, Bitcoin block, scannable verify QR), and on the camera-scope question said to double-check because they thought journal entries already had a camera.

I double-checked and grounded the camera answer honestly: there is no in-app camera. The composer 'photo' button is a plain file input with accept=image/* and no capture attribute — on a phone the OS picker offers 'Take Photo' through the system camera, but the app never runs getUserMedia, so there's no live preview or selfie toggle. A true in-app camera is a separate build. I told the operator that and proceeded with the stamping, which works on any photo regardless of how it arrived.

The cut itself: I extracted the proof-mint + verify-URL logic out of QuickShareModal into a reusable buildVerifyUrl.ts (returns json + verifyUrl + urlIsInline) and refactored QuickShareModal to use it, so the Fresh share card and the new photo QR build the identical one-tap /verify link and can't drift. stampPhoto.ts draws the displayed image onto a canvas and burns a translucent corner panel carrying the Tapit mark, capture date, who captured it, the Bitcoin block once confirmed (or 'Anchoring to Bitcoin…' until then), and a QR rendered from a dynamically-imported qrcode so the library only loads when someone actually stamps. The QR encodes a multiDisclosureProof disclosing the attachment_sha256 leaf plus written_at, so a scanner lands on /verify with the proof loaded and can re-hash the photo to confirm it's the signed-and-anchored one. I added a shareFile helper to share.ts using the Web Share API Level 2 files pathway (system sheet incl. AirDrop / Save-to-Files) with a download fallback, and StampedPhotoButton ties it together under the image in JournalDetail with a clear note that the original is left untouched. Manifests and the living-ideas log updated; all four gates green, 575 tests, JournalDetail chunk 7.25KB gz under its 8KB budget with qrcode staying its own on-demand chunk.
narrative.whats_pending:
Zero device validation. The operator should open a journal entry that has a photo on the phone, tap 'Share a stamped copy', and confirm the badge reads cleanly in the corner — that the QR scans from a normal viewing distance, that the text is legible over a real photo (the panel is translucent dark with white/lime text, but it's unverified against a bright or busy image), and that the system share sheet carries the actual JPEG file (Web Share Level 2 file support is good on modern iOS but the download fallback path is what fires on desktop). The badge sizes everything off the short edge of the image; very small or very wide images haven't been eyeballed.

The big captured follow-on is the in-app camera / selfie capture — the operator expected one to exist. A getUserMedia live-preview camera with a front/back toggle that flows straight into normalizeImage -> sign -> anchor -> optional auto-stamp would make 'take it through the app and it stamps it' literal, and it pairs directly with this cut. It's logged in ideas.md as the sprouting follow-on. Also deferred there: a light always-on cosmetic brand mark baked into the bytes at capture, as a toggle, if the operator later wants a permanent always-visible look in addition to the verifiable shared copy.

The QR will silently drop (text-only badge) if the inline proof exceeds QR capacity — stampPhoto catches the qrcode throw and degrades. For the small attachment_sha256 + written_at disclosure that should never happen, but it's worth watching that the verify link still travels in the share text in that degraded case (today it does not — the text path only carries the file; if the QR ever drops, the verify URL is lost from that share). That's a small honest gap if disclosure ever grows.
narrative.what_you_could_do_better:
One honest gap I'd flag for the next carpenter: when the QR degrades (proof too big for a QR), the stamped image loses its verify link entirely, because the share carries only the file, not accompanying text with the URL. For the current tiny disclosure this never triggers, so I left it rather than over-building, but if the disclosed-paths set ever grows, the right move is to also pass the verify URL as share text alongside the file (the way QuickShareModal does for the over-budget case). I chose not to pre-solve a case that can't happen yet, but I'm naming it so it isn't a silent trap later.

The other thing worth watching is altitude on the camera question — the operator thought a camera existed, and the correct move was to verify against the actual input element rather than trust the feature's own manifest, which describes the file button as a 'camera shortcut.' That manifest phrasing is arguably what seeded the operator's belief; I updated it to be explicit that there is no live camera, which should prevent the next person (or the operator) from re-inferring a camera that isn't there.
narrative.bigger_picture: This cut is the experience-is-the-moat thesis pointed at proof portability. The wallet already had everything needed to prove a photo — the hash is signed, the signature is anchored to Bitcoin, the /verify route re-runs the math with no server trust — but that proof lived in a separate share card or a pasted JSON bundle, detached from the photo itself. Burning the verify QR and the human-readable provenance into the corner of the image makes the proof travel WITH the artifact, which is how images actually move through the world: screenshotted, forwarded, re-shared, stripped of metadata. EXIF and embedded metadata get destroyed by every messaging app's re-encode; a visible, scannable mark composited into the pixels survives exactly that gauntlet. And the deliberate choice to stamp a copy rather than the signed original keeps the two concerns clean — the canonical signed bytes stay the source of cryptographic truth, while the stamped copy is a derived, shareable proof object, the same division the wallet already draws between a held attestation and the disclosure proof minted from it. The reusable buildVerifyUrl extraction is a small instance of the durable-interface principle: one way to turn an attestation into a one-tap verify link, consumed by every surface that needs it. The north-star extension the operator already named — an in-app camera that captures, signs, anchors, and stamps in one motion — would close the loop from 'a photo I happen to have' to 'a photo born verifiable inside the wallet,' which is the sovereign-capture story the whole chassis is building toward.

questions_asked.question: How should the corner stamp relate to the actual saved photo?
questions_asked.carpenters_read: Preserve the signed + anchored original; composite the badge onto a copy at share time. Lets the badge show the live Bitcoin block + a real verify QR, and keeps file-integrity simple.

questions_asked.question: What should the corner mark actually show?
questions_asked.carpenters_read: Full provenance + a scannable proof. Built all four into the badge; the QR is the load-bearing one (re-runs the math), the text is human context.

feedback_to_appcommander: Two patterns worth lifting. First, the grounding discipline paid off twice this session: the operator asked 'is it possible to stamp the photo' and 'isn't there already a camera,' and both answers depended on reading the actual photo pipeline and the actual input element rather than the feature's own manifest prose — which in fact described the file button as a 'camera shortcut,' the likely seed of the operator's belief that a camera existed. Worth a doctrine note: when the operator asks whether a capability exists, verify against the code that implements it, not the manifest that describes it, and fix the manifest if its phrasing is what misled. Second, this is a clean example of surfacing a real architectural fork in chip form instead of silently choosing: the bake-into-signed-bytes vs stamp-a-copy decision has genuine cryptographic consequences (digest definition, whether the badge can show the async-confirmed block, whether a self-referencing QR is even possible), and laying those out as the chip descriptions let the operator make an informed call in one tap. The reusable buildVerifyUrl extraction (one attestation-to-verify-link path consumed by every surface) is the durable-interface-over-duplication principle in miniature and is the kind of small refactor worth doing inline whenever a second consumer of copy-pasted logic appears.
